title: Λέων ⟨λυσσῶν⟩ καὶ ἔλαφος
titleEn: The Mad Lion and the Deer
part: The Mad Lion and the Deer (Chambry 212)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 212. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.n: λυσσάω is the verb of rabies — the madness that takes a dog — and the imperfect sets it as a standing condition, not a single fit. In the title Chambry prints ⟨λυσσῶν⟩ in angle brackets, his mark for a word he himself supplies.

sentences.t: Τοῦτον δὲ ἔλαφος ἐξ ὕλης ἰδὼν εἶπεν· « Οὐαὶ ἡμῖν τοῖς ταλαιπώροις· τί γὰρ μαινόμενος οὗτος οὐχὶ ποιήσει, ὃς καὶ σωφρονῶν οὐκ ἦν ἡμῖν φορητός; »
sentences.tr: Touton de elaphos ex hylēs idōn eipen· « Ouai hēmin tois talaipōrois· ti gar mainomenos houtos ouchi poiēsei, hos kai sōphronōn ouk ēn hēmin phorētos; »
sentences.l: And a deer, having-seen him from the wood, said: « Woe to us wretched ones; for what will this one, raving, not do, who even being-of-sound-mind was not bearable to us? »
sentences.i: A deer saw him from the wood and said: « Woe to us poor creatures! What will he not do in his madness, when even in his right mind he was more than we could bear? »
sentences.n: Οὐαί is a cry of lament, common in the Greek of the Septuagint and rare in classical prose. μαινόμενος and σωφρονῶν are the standing pair of opposites — out of one's mind against sound of mind. μαινόμενος states the circumstance the deer now faces, "in his madness"; σωφρονῶν, with καί before it, is the concessive one, "even when he was in his right mind". φορητός is a verbal adjective, "such as can be borne".

sentences.t: Ὅτι τοὺς θυμώδεις ἄνδρας καὶ ἀδικεῖν εἰθισμένους πάντες φευγέτωσαν ἀρχὴν λαβόντας καὶ δυναστεύσαντας.
sentences.tr: Hoti tous thymōdeis andras kai adikein eithismenous pantes pheugetōsan archēn labontas kai dynasteusantas.
sentences.l: That all are-to-flee hot-tempered men and ones accustomed to do-wrong, once these have-taken office and have-come-to-power.
sentences.i: The story shows that all are to flee hot-tempered men, men accustomed to doing wrong, once they have taken office and come to power.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. φευγέτωσαν is a third-person imperative, "let them flee", which English carries with "are to". The single article τούς covers both θυμώδεις and εἰθισμένους — one set of men described twice, not two sets. The aorist participles λαβόντας and δυναστεύσαντας are accusative, agreeing with those men and not with πάντες, and they name the moment the danger begins: not the temper itself but the temper with power behind it.
